newsitem.title: GERMANY: Salomon restates "buy" tip on Thyssen.
newsitem.headline: Salomon restates "buy" tip on Thyssen.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers on Tuesday restated a "buy" recommendation for shares in German steel group Thyssen AG, which is target of a hostile takeover bid by the rival Krupp group.
Salomon also issued a buy recommendation for Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, but that position is under review pending details of the takeover bid.
Salomon's European steel analyst Terence Sinclair said in a research note that if the bid is successful it would open up "extensive synergies" between the two companies.
But he warned that highly-indebted Krupp would "have to gear itself up massively" to finance the takeover by issuing new shares.

Sinclair estimated Krupp's market capitalisation at 5.9 billion marks ($3.5 billion) and its net debt at 2.9 billion marks. Thyssen's capitalisation is 10.8 billion marks, it carries 3.6 billion marks in net debt and 6.1 billion marks in other liabilities.

He said Krupp would be able to earn between six and seven billion marks in disposals -- mainly of Thyssen's E-Plus mobile telephone interests -- but that would leave a price tag of between eight and 12 billion marks left to finance.
"This will be a very considerable stretch. Krupp will have to finance the deal with shares," he said.
He added that if the deal is financed imaginatively, there was considerable upside for the Krupp share price. If not, the target would be "indigestible" and the price may be too great.

Krupp's shares were suspended from the Frankfurt bourse on Tuesday after closing bourse trade on Monday 272 marks, while Thyssen were suspended at 346.80 marks. Thyssen shares climbed to around 400 marks in grey market trade after the suspension.
Sinclair said the hostile bid would create synergies in steel and automotive operations as well as allowing reductions in the workforce.
Closing Krupp's Dortmund flat carbon steel plant, which lost 200 million marks last year, could alone be worth up to 100 marks on the company's share price.
Upstream synergies in coke and iron production could save 200 to 300 million marks a year. Plans by both companies to build thin slab casters would give way to one project.

The two companies' automotive operations, with combined turnover of 7.5 billion marks last year, show weak profits. Sinclair said cost synergies of 100 million marks could be achieved quickly, "with much greater prizes long term".
With a combined workforce of over 195,000 there would be scope for job reductions. A reduction of 10,000 workers would double pre-tax margins.
But, Sinclair added: "Since many jobs would go with restructuring, there would be tens of thousands of redundancies with massive political consequences."

In addition to requiring European regulatory approval, the deal could face strong resistance from Krupp's own workforce -- which is represented on the supervisory board -- and the ruling Social Democrats in Dortmund, the base of Krupp's steel operations, he said.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.690 German Marks)
